title: A Visitor for the Harvest
premise: Theo Brightwater hosts a midnight call-in show from a farmhouse studio, taking calls from listeners who died the week before—until the dead start calling about Theo's own family. The Brightwater house, inherited from a grandmother Theo never met, keeps its occupants invisible to something that walks the frost line each autumn, and the mirrors' one-second delay is the first crack in that protection. As Theo's found family of insomniac listeners gathers at the house, they learn the harvest song their grandmother wrote holds the terms of the inheritance: sing all three verses and be claimed, refuse it and be taken. In the end, Theo discovers a fourth verse hidden in the radio static—a verse of refusal written for them—and by broadcasting it on air, breaks the contract, freeing the house and the dead who lingered in its debt.
about_author: Wren Okonkwo is a former late-night radio producer who grew up in farm country where the local stations signed off at midnight and nobody asked why. Their fiction explores what families owe each other after death, and how much truth loyalty can survive.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. On the anniversary broadcast of 'The Night Line,' Theo takes a call from Marisol, a devoted listener—and realizes mid-conversation that Marisol died four days ago. The emotional beat is quiet dread wrapped in professional calm; Theo keeps talking because hanging up feels like abandonment.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo returns to the inherited Brightwater farmhouse and follows grandmother Edith's strange rules taped inside cabinets: count the doors nightly, keep every light burning, never sing past the second verse. The beat is uneasy belonging—Theo has no other home, so the rules feel like care and captivity at once.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A mirror shows Theo raising a coffee cup a full second before Theo does it. Testing every reflective surface, Theo finds the delay growing. The beat is vertigo—the house is out of sync with itself, and Theo can't tell which version is real.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Theo and Dev, an insomniac listener. Dev calls in describing the same mirror lag in his own apartment across town. Two lonely people realize they're hearing the same thing. The beat is cautious connection—found family beginning as shared symptom.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In the attic, Theo finds Edith's ledger listing names, dates of death, and a column labeled 'paid.' Every name matches a caller on the Night Line. The beat is betrayal—Theo's inheritance isn't a house but a collection route, and the dead have been paying into it.

chapters.title: The Song in the Walls
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev arrives at the farmhouse seeking answers and hears humming inside the plaster—three verses, always stopping before the last. The beat is wonder curdling into fear as he realizes the house itself knows the melody and wants someone to finish it.

chapters.title: Frost Line
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. First frost. From the porch, Theo watches a figure walk the property line exactly where the frost ends, pausing at each window. It doesn't cross. The beat is terror with a strange comfort: the rules work, but only barely, and winter is long.

chapters.title: The Listeners Come Home
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating through Dev, Ruthie (a widow caller), and Marcus (a trucker). Drawn by dreams of the song, three listeners arrive at the farmhouse uninvited. The beat is friction turning to warmth—strangers arguing over whose grief is worse, then cooking dinner together anyway.

chapters.title: What Marisol Wanted
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Marisol's voice comes through the farmhouse radio without being called, asking Ruthie to deliver a message to her daughter. The beat is tenderness and moral weight—the dead aren't monsters here, they're clients, and helping them may violate Edith's rules.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus finds his own name in Edith's ledger with tomorrow's date beside it. He tries to leave; the road loops back to the porch. The beat is panic and resignation—he was recruited, not rescued, and the family he found may be a trap.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev, a former choir kid, transcribes the humming and recognizes it as a harvest hymn Edith once performed locally. Researching, he learns every choir that sang it fully disbanded within a year. The beat is scholarly dread—knowledge is getting closer to danger.

chapters.title: Mirrors Forward
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The delay reverses: now the mirrors show the room one second ahead. Theo sees themselves singing something they haven't sung yet. The beat is fatalism—the house isn't malfunctioning; it's rehearsing Theo for a role already written.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Desperate to speak with her dead husband properly, Ruthie offers to sing the third verse if the house lets him stay. The lights flicker agreement. The beat is heartbreak—love weaponized against the group, and no villain, just grief.

chapters.title: The Door Count Fails
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The nightly count returns thirteen doors in a twelve-door house. Something new is inside, wearing the shape of the extra door. The beat is siege horror—the protections weren't keeping it out; they were keeping score.

chapters.title: Edith Speaks
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Through the studio microphone, Edith's voice finally addresses Theo directly: she didn't write the song, she inherited it, and the last verse is the price of exit—one singer per generation, chosen by whoever the frost reaches first. The beat is generational reckoning—Theo was named before birth.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus proposes they all sing the third verse together to split the debt. Ruthie refuses—her bargain is personal. Dev argues the ledger proves sharing doesn't dilute anything. The beat is the theme made explicit: loyalty to each other versus loyalty to the truth of what the house demands.

chapters.title: The Frost Reaches In
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The frost crosses the line for the first time, writing patterns up the windows like sheet music. Ruthie begins the third verse at midnight, her husband's voice joining hers. The beat is climax-in-motion—the contract activating, the house exhaling after decades of holding its breath.

chapters.title: Static Verse
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Tuning the shortwave desperately, Dev finds a fourth verse buried in static—Edith's handwriting in audio form, recorded the night she died: a verse of refusal, unsingable alone. The beat is desperate hope—the inheritance includes the tools of escape, hidden in plain signal.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Climax. Theo takes the Night Line live, plays Edith's fourth verse over the air, and asks every listener—living and dead—to hum along without singing the words. The frost stops mid-pattern. The house, built on a solo contract, cannot enforce a chorus of refusal. The beat is defiant communion.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Show Now
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Morning. The mirrors are simply mirrors. Ruthie's husband is gone—not freed, gone—and she must decide whether the trade was worth breaking. The beat is bittersweet cost: victory that doesn't refund what grief already spent.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo broadcasts one final Night Line, thanking the callers by name, then signs off forever. The dead don't call again. The beat is mourning the strange intimacy of the show even as its purpose ends.

chapters.title: A Visitor for the Harvest
chapters.summary: Epilogue, ensemble POV. One year later, the found family gathers at the farmhouse for a harvest dinner, doors counted out of habit rather than fear. When frost writes on the window, it spells only 'thank you.' The beat is earned peace—inheritance rewritten as choice, family kept not by contract but by showing up.
